title: The talking mind
hookLine: brain areas busy during mind-wandering were quieter in experienced meditators in a 2011 study (Brewer et al.)
carry: you are the one hearing it

lines: A RADIO IN THE NEXT ROOM.
cards: You're brushing your teeth. Nobody is talking to you. And yet there's talking.
Should have said that differently in the meeting. What's for dinner. Why did she text like that.
Remember to buy batteries. It's a radio you never switched on, playing in the next room, mostly about you. It can seem like that's just what a mind is.
In 2011 a team at Yale got curious, and put experienced meditators into a brain scanner to see what happens to that radio when people practice.

teach.b: First, the brain. Around the turn of this century, researchers noticed that when people lie in a scanner doing nothing in particular, certain brain areas get busier, not quieter.
They called this the default mode network: what the brain does by default. It's busy when we daydream, replay the past, plan, and think about ourselves.

In the 2011 study, Judson Brewer and colleagues scanned a small group of experienced meditators and a group of beginners. During meditation, key parts of that network were less active in the experienced group.
Small study, one snapshot; remember compared to what. It doesn't prove meditation rewires anyone, but it fits what meditation teachers have described. Second, the stream.
William James, the American psychologist, wrote in 1890 that thinking is not a chain or a train of separate pieces.

teach.h: IT IS NOTHING JOINTED; IT FLOWS.
teach.b: In his words, "It is nothing jointed; it flows." A stream, he said, is the natural picture. You don't turn a stream off.
You can sit on the bank. Third, the old noticing.
Some meditation teachers, notably in Buddhist insight practice, teach a simple move: when a thought grabs you, name it softly. Thinking. Planning.
Worrying. The naming makes a small gap between you and the voice. You are the one hearing it, so you're not only the voice.
The talking mind isn't an enemy. It plans dinners and solves problems. But much of its chatter is rehearsal and replay, and some of it has a tone you'd notice at once if anyone else used it on you.
You can't unplug the radio. You can notice it's on, and turn it down a notch.

how: Some meditation teachers, notably in Buddhist insight practice, teach noting: when a thought arises, the meditator names it softly, such as thinking or planning, and returns to the breath.

o: a researcher who scanned experienced meditators' brains
a doctor who first recorded brain waves during sleep
a teacher who brought silent retreats to the West

games.q: the talking mind — tap the pairs.
p: it is nothing jointed; it flows

s: the brain goes quiet when you're doing nothing
some areas, the default mode network, get busier when we're idle.
the 2011 study proves meditation rewires the brain
it was a small snapshot study; it fits the picture, but proves no such thing.
William James compared thought to a stream
in 1890 he wrote that thinking flows, and isn't jointed like a chain.

games.q: you sit to practice, and the voice in your head starts replaying an argument. what do some meditation teachers suggest?
o: name it softly, then return to the breath.
stop meditating: you're doing it wrong.
games.why: noting: call it replaying or thinking, and come back. the thought showing up isn't failure; noticing it is the practice.

practice: Listen to your own inner talk the way you'd overhear a stranger on a bus, without arguing or trying to make it stop. Skip the content and listen for the tone: is it kind, hurried, bossy, and whose voice does it sound like?
When you've heard enough, come back to one breath, then listen again.

wordCard.voice: Brewer, whose 2011 scan found the stream of inner chatter quieted in experienced meditators.

carryVoice: Your line: you are the one hearing it. The radio can play on in the next room. See you tomorrow.
